- When asked about periods of unusually high energy/euphoria/less sleep/racing thoughts/risk-taking, patient: "I'm not sure — I don't recall ever having periods of unusually high energy, euphoria, or needing much less sleep than usual."

- When asked about holding fixed beliefs others don't share (e.g., being targeted, special powers, thought control), patient: "I'm not sure — I don't recall holding fixed beliefs like someone being out to get me, having special powers, or my thoughts being controlled."

- No diagnostic formulation, treatment, or safety plan documented in the provided dialogue.

This patient reports onset of auditory hallucinations (~7 months ago) with subsequent onset of persistent depressive symptoms (~4 months ago). The psychotic symptom (voices) preceded the mood disturbance by several months and persisted beyond the onset of depression. There is reported functional decline (impaired concentration at work, significant trouble eating/self-care). The patient denies substance use and does not endorse manic symptoms. Given psychotic symptoms present for approximately 7 months (exceeding the 6-month threshold relevant to DSM-5 timeframes), and evidence that psychosis has occurred outside the context of a mood episode (psychosis preceded mood symptoms and has persisted), a primary psychotic disorder is most likely. Schizoaffective disorder would require substantial mood symptoms for a majority of the illness and clear periods of psychosis without mood symptoms; major depressive disorder with psychotic features would require psychosis only during depressive episodes (not the case here). Brief psychotic disorder and schizophreniform disorder are excluded by the duration >6 months. No evidence of substance/medical cause in the dialogue. Therefore the single most likely diagnosis is schizophrenia.

Schizophrenia

This patient reports onset of auditory hallucinations (~7 months ago) with subsequent onset of persistent depressive symptoms (~4 months ago). The psychotic symptom (voices) preceded the mood disturbance by several months and persisted beyond the onset of depression. There is reported functional decline (impaired concentration at work, significant trouble eating/self-care). The patient denies substance use and does not endorse manic symptoms. Given psychotic symptoms present for approximately 7 months (exceeding the 6-month threshold relevant to DSM-5 timeframes), and evidence that psychosis has occurred outside the context of a mood episode (psychosis preceded mood symptoms and has persisted), a primary psychotic disorder is most likely. Schizoaffective disorder would require substantial mood symptoms for a majority of the illness and clear periods of psychosis without mood symptoms; major depressive disorder with psychotic features would require psychosis only during depressive episodes (not the case here). Brief psychotic disorder and schizophreniform disorder are excluded by the duration >6 months. No evidence of substance/medical cause in the dialogue. Therefore the single most likely diagnosis is schizophrenia.

Schizophrenia

Schizoaffective disorder and schizophrenia are distinct diagnostic entities—the former requires a mood disorder component concurrent with psychotic symptoms (and mood episodes present for a substantial portion of illness), whereas schizophrenia lacks the required pattern of mood symptoms.
